newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asian buyers sit back, focus on Philippines.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian buyers sit back, focus on Philippines.

text.p: The Southeast Asian grains and oilseeds market was quiet with the trade waiting for news on when the Philippines would tender for an estimated 155,000 tonnes of corn for July arrival, dealers said on Thursday.
"We're waiting for the Philippine government to set a date for the corn tender," a dealer for a European commodity house said. "That seems to be the only spot news on the horizon."

Philippine Agriculture Undersecretary Joemari Gerochi said last week Manila is planning to import at least 300,000 tonnes of corn before July to meet the needs of its rapidly growing livestock and poultry industry.
The country has already bought 120,000 tonnes of yellow corn from China and 25,000 tonnes of white corn from the U.S. since the beginning of the year.
"People are waiting for the Philippine tender. There's no business being done in the nearbys at the moment," a dealer for a U.S. commodity house said.

U.S. corn coming into Southeast Asia was seen at US$142-$143 a tonne C&F on a Panamax for June/July shipment. Argentine corn was quoted a shade lower at $138-$140 on the same basis while Chinese corn ranged between $141-$144 a tonne C&F.
Buyers were said to be holding back to watch how weather conditions in the U.S. affect the new corn and soybean crop and to wait for a break in Chicago futures prices, dealers said.

Indonesia is said to have open positions in July for 50,000 tonnes of soymeal while Thailand may be in for about 20,000 tonnes. Malaysia has more than ample coverage and is currently out of the market, dealers said.
"It's still a waiting game," another dealer said. "People are waiting for the last minute before deciding to buy."
Firm cash prices in the U.S. and Argentina are also keeping most buyers sidelined. "The premiums are very strong in Argentina," one dealer said.
The attention of buyers in Indonesia, who already have ample coverage, remain focused on the country's elections next week.
"Some of the people there are out campaigning or helping out," one said. "It's quiet everywhere, but especially in Indonesia."
One analyst said buyers will take some time before coming back into the market until they get a clearer idea of the U.S. corn and soybean crop.
"For new crop, we're just watching the weather. It's going to be another six weeks before we get a good idea of what the crop looks like," the analyst said.
"There's usually a high correlation between a good planting pace and high yields. But it's been a very cold spring and we don't know how that will affect the crop," the analyst added.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) said last Monday that 88 percent of the U.S. corn crop has been planted versus the 67 percent five year average. About 46 percent of the soybean crop was planted against the five year average of 26.
Regional traders said the only time buyers will come back will be if futures prices on Chicago tumble in the near-term.
"Nobody wants to be a hero and rush in," a dealer said.
